newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: Mercy for Venezuela pay deal may spark bolsa rally.
newsitem.headline: Mercy for Venezuela pay deal may spark bolsa rally.

text.p: Might there after all be a grain of compassion lurking amid the cold calculations and crackling knuckles of world financial markets?
Normally, international investors would have punished Venezuela's recent 35 percent public sector pay rise offer with a stock market selloff, taking the hike as a government cave-in to union power.

Yet, bucking the trend, the Caracas bolsa's leading .IBC index looks to have reversed its January slump, moving ahead nearly four percent since Finance Minister Luis Raul Matos Azocar outlined the wage proposal Wednesday.
His offer -- provisionally accepted by the country's largest union, the Confederation of Venezuelan Workers -- also includes a 50 percent increase in monthly bonuses.
"It's not yet a buying panic ... But investor interest in Venezuelan shares has definitely picked up," said New York-based Credit Lyonnais broker Peter Ryan.
The market's apparent mercy stems from the promise of social peace that a public sector pay deal could bring, analysts say, not from improving macroeconomic indicators.
"We never thought the government's original 25 percent pay offer would swing with the unions after inflation wasted real wages last year," said a lead economist at one of the largest U.S. banks.
Venezuelan inflation hit 103 percent in 1996 and is seen at between 25 and 30 percent this year according to governemnt targets, although analysts put it upwards of 35 percent.
"People were worried about riots. Hopefully that's been put to rest by the pay offer, opening the way for a deepening of the economic reform program," he added.
Last year, the Caracas bolsa was the world's best performing, broadly rising over 100 percent in dollar terms. This year, gains will be more selective, analysts say.

Inflationary pressures, stemming from rising consumer demand on the back of wage increase, "will probably force the Central Bank to keep up its strong bolivar policy to help beat down prices," said Santander analyst Jose Corral.
Corral sees the bolivar appreciating 20 percent in real terms through 1997. That would penalize exporters such as steel company Sivensa and Sudamtex.

But it would also favor companies with dollar-denominated debts and high local sales, especially market leaders Electricidad de Caracas and telephone company CANTV. "They're two of our favorites for the year," said InvestAnalysis analyst Daniel Lahoud. After slipping in January, both stocks are now up some eight percent on the year.

Public spending is seen growing by an estimated one percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) on the wage hike, boosting economic growth to upwards of four percent even as ministers say the budget can accomodate the expenditure increase.
Amid such conditions, foods company Mavesa should see sales surge. "But it's a rather expensive stock at the moment," added Lahoud.

Financial shares are also seen lagging after they lead the market's rise in 1996. InvestAnalysis counts a number of banks among its "untouchables" for 1997, including Banco Venezolano de Credito, Banco Mercantil A shares and Banco Provincial.
